scope: Requirement lifecycle: spec req, spec supersede, spec amend, and @-refs. Belongs here: next-id allocation; non-interactive authoring; supersede, move, and amend; @path file-ref resolution. Does not belong here: scaffolding a domain (DOMAIN). Boundary case: minting a requirement id is REQ; scaffolding the domain that holds it is DOMAIN.

requirements.statement: spec req <domain-prefix> resolves its prefix case-insensitively against the domains found on the filesystem, uppercasing the input and stripping whitespace before matching.
requirements.why: Requiring the exact uppercased key before an id can be minted is friction with no safety gain; resolving case-insensitively against the real domain listing removes it without guessing a domain.

requirements.statement: spec req <domain-prefix> resolves to the domain whose key exactly equals the input when one exists, and otherwise to the single domain the input is a unique prefix of.
requirements.why: Without exact-match precedence, `auth` would be ambiguous whenever both AUTH and AUTHX exist, blocking the author from the domain they plainly named.

requirements.statement: spec req <domain-prefix> prints the matching candidate domains to stderr and exits 2 when the prefix matches more than one domain and none matches exactly.
requirements.why: Silently choosing one of several matching domains would mint the id in the wrong domain — a requirement authored into BOOKING when the author meant BILLING is a durable mistake.

requirements.statement: spec req <domain-prefix> prints the available domains to stderr and exits 2 when the prefix matches no existing domain, and never mints a <KEY>-001 id for a domain that does not exist.
requirements.why: Minting an id for a non-existent domain would create a requirement with no SPEC.json to hold it; domain creation belongs to spec domain new, kept separate so a typo cannot silently birth a domain.

requirements.statement: spec req <domain-prefix>, run non-interactively with piped stdin, prints the next unused id — the domain's SPEC.json max sequence + 1, padded to three digits, as <KEY>-<NNN> on stdout — and exits 0.
requirements.why: IDs are never reused; the id query must agree with the domain envelope's requirements, not a regex approximation.

requirements.statement: spec req on a non-platform directory prints the friendly not-a-platform message and exits 2.
requirements.why: Same command-boundary pattern as map/index/check.

requirements.statement: Exit codes across the authoring surfaces are 0 and 2 only; exit 1 stays reserved for spec check --ci semantic failures.
requirements.why: CI must be able to distinguish gate failures from authoring/usage errors.

requirements.statement: When stdin is a TTY, spec req enters the interactive per-field prompt flow with prompts rendered to stderr; the allocated id and Active status are displayed but not editable.
requirements.why: stdout stays machine-parseable while humans author interactively.

requirements.statement: When stdin is not a TTY, spec req prints the next unused id and exits 0 — no prompts, no writes, no readline.
requirements.why: The composable id query for scripts and agents is preserved byte-for-byte.
requirements.deprecatedReason: Duplicate of REQ-005: both state the non-TTY id-query contract; the no-prompts/no-writes clause is folded into the rewritten REQ-005. Retag req.ts sites from REQ-009 to REQ-005.

requirements.statement: spec req, in its interactive TTY flow, aborts with a stderr notice and exit 0 writing zero bytes when the author submits an empty Requirement statement.
requirements.why: Following the git-editor convention, an abandoned authoring session must be a clean no-op — treating an empty statement as a save would persist a meaningless entry.

requirements.statement: spec req <KEY> --text appends a new Active requirement to the domain's SPEC.json — status active, the given statement, why null, empty relates/livesIn/issues, changedAtVersion 1 — and bumps the envelope's updated to the local date, such that the appended entry re-indexes with zero diagnostics.
requirements.why: Authoring must produce exactly what the indexer ingests, or authored requirements silently vanish.

requirements.statement: An @-ref is @<relative/path> preceded by start-of-string or whitespace, containing at least one slash, resolved against the platform root; emails, @spec tags, and version pins never match.
requirements.why: Requirement text points at code without false positives on everyday @ usage.

requirements.statement: spec req scans each authored field for an @-prefixed relative-path code reference and, when that path does not resolve under the platform root, warns on stderr while still saving the requirement.
requirements.why: A requirement may legitimately point at code that does not exist yet; blocking the save on an unresolved reference would stop authors from recording intent ahead of implementation.

requirements.statement: spec term authors, lists, and revises glossary TERM entries (definition in the statement, headword in term, synonyms in aliases), and spec supersede/amend operate on TERM ids exactly as on requirements — carrying term/aliases through the successor and amend shapes.
requirements.why: Terms are lifecycle-managed like requirements: a shift in meaning must supersede (or revise-with-bump), never silently redefine; reusing the one lifecycle machinery keeps a term and a requirement governed by the same guarantees.

requirements.statement: spec amend refuses any requirement that has at least one bound @spec tag; amend is permitted only for a Draft entry or an Active entry with zero bound tags, and once code tags a requirement, spec supersede is the sole path that may change it.
requirements.why: amend rewrites a requirement in place with no version bump, so amending a requirement that code already binds would silently mutate shipped truth out from under the @spec tags that verify it, leaving no supersede trail recording that the meaning changed.

requirements.statement: spec supersede and spec move take every version they emit — the --json spec_version for supersede, the source and target versions for move, and the persisted supersededAtVersion died-at stamp — from the freshly-reindexed supersede DAG, never from an incremented authored envelope counter.
requirements.why: If these commands emitted or stamped a self-incremented authored number, the version a lineage records and an agent parses would diverge from the DAG-derived number that pins, drift, and gate compare against, resurrecting the two-sources-of-truth split the derived model exists to close.

requirements.statement: spec req <KEY> --text appends a new Active requirement to the domain's SPEC.json — status active, the given statement, why null when unset, empty relates/livesIn/issues, and no authored version counter — and bumps the envelope's updated to the local date, such that the appended entry re-indexes with zero diagnostics.
requirements.why: Authoring must produce exactly what the indexer ingests, or authored requirements silently vanish.

requirements.statement: When allocating the next requirement id, the system shall take the maximum sequence over both the working-tree spec and the spec at git HEAD, so a deleted entry's id is never re-minted.
requirements.why: An id freed by deletion gets reassigned to unrelated behavior, and every existing tag and reference then points at the wrong requirement.

requirements.statement: The spec CLI shall expose neither a spec new nor a spec id subcommand.
requirements.why: The noun-verb surface (spec domain new, spec req) replaced them; resurrecting the old spellings would fork the authoring path into two diverging front doors.
requirements.deprecatedReason: States the absence of removed commands (history, rule 5).

requirements.statement: When new statement text is authored into a domain that declares the ears grammar, the spec CLI shall judge it against the EARS shapes — warning and writing under warning severity, refusing the write under error severity.
requirements.why: Catching a malformed statement at write time costs one message; catching it after code binds to the id costs a supersede.

requirements.statement: When spec deprecate is run with a reason on an Active or Draft requirement, the spec CLI shall set the entry's status to deprecated, record the reason on the entry, and list every code tag still bound to the id.
requirements.why: Without a command, end-of-life was a hand edit with the reason lost in a code comment that dies with the code — the entry itself is the only place the reason survives deletion.

requirements.statement: When resolving its domain-prefix argument, spec req shall uppercase the input and strip whitespace, matching case-insensitively against the domains enumerated from the filesystem.
requirements.why: Requiring the exact uppercased key before an id can be minted is friction with no safety gain; case-insensitive resolution against the real listing removes it without guessing a domain.

requirements.statement: When resolving a domain prefix, spec req shall prefer an exact key match over prefix matching, resolving a non-exact input only when it is a unique prefix of a single domain.
requirements.why: Without exact-match precedence, auth would be ambiguous whenever both AUTH and AUTHX exist, blocking the author from the domain they plainly named.

requirements.statement: If a domain prefix matches more than one domain and none exactly, then spec req shall print the candidate domains to stderr and exit 2.
requirements.why: Silently choosing one of several matching domains would mint the id in the wrong domain — a requirement authored into BOOKING when the author meant BILLING is a durable mistake.

requirements.statement: If a domain prefix matches no existing domain, then spec req shall print the available domains to stderr and exit 2, never minting a <KEY>-001 id for a domain that does not exist.
requirements.why: Minting an id for a non-existent domain would create a requirement with no SPEC.json to hold it; domain creation stays with spec domain new so a typo cannot silently birth a domain.

requirements.statement: When stdin is not a TTY, spec req <domain-prefix> shall print only the next unused id — the domain's maximum sequence number plus one, padded to three digits, as <KEY>-<NNN> — on stdout and exit 0, with no prompts and no writes.
requirements.why: Ids are never reused, so the id query must agree with the domain envelope itself, not a regex approximation; a prompt or a write in the piped path breaks every script and agent that composes it.

requirements.statement: If spec req is run against a directory containing no spec-engine/ directory, then it shall print the friendly not-a-platform guidance and exit 2.
requirements.why: A raw throw at the platform boundary buries the fix; exit 2 keeps the usage error distinct from the exit-1 code CI reserves for check --ci gate failures.

requirements.statement: The authoring commands — spec req / domain / supersede / amend / deprecate — shall exit only 0 or 2, leaving exit 1 reserved for spec check --ci data-level failures.
requirements.why: A CI script branching on exit codes would misread an authoring usage error as a spec-gate failure if the authoring surface ever emitted exit 1.

requirements.statement: While stdin is a TTY, spec req shall run its per-field authoring prompts on stderr, displaying the allocated id and Active status as fixed, non-editable values.
requirements.why: Prompts on stdout would corrupt the machine-parseable channel scripts consume, and an editable id would let an author collide with the allocator's next-unused guarantee.

requirements.statement: If the author submits an empty Requirement statement in the interactive flow, then spec req shall abort with a stderr notice and exit 0, writing zero bytes.
requirements.why: Following the git-editor convention, an abandoned session must be a clean no-op — treating an empty statement as a save would persist a meaningless entry.

requirements.statement: When scanning requirement text for @-refs, the engine shall match @<relative/path> only when preceded by start-of-string or whitespace and containing at least one slash, resolving it against the platform root and never matching emails, @spec tags, or version pins.
requirements.why: Requirement text points at code; a looser pattern would flag everyday @ usage (emails, tags, pins) as broken file references and drown the real ones in noise.

requirements.statement: When an authored field carries an @-prefixed path that does not resolve under the platform root, spec req shall warn on stderr and still save the requirement.
requirements.why: A requirement may legitimately point at code that does not exist yet; blocking the save would stop authors from recording intent ahead of implementation.

requirements.statement: Where a glossary term is authored via spec term, the engine shall store it as a requirement row — definition in statement, headword in term, synonyms in aliases — never in a parallel schema.
requirements.why: A parallel term schema would need its own lifecycle, index path, and drift logic, all free to diverge from the one set of guarantees requirements already carry.
requirements.deprecatedReason: Storage-model statement (never in a parallel schema); terms' observable behavior is in REQ-034 and the TERM commands.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec amend targets a TERM id, it shall operate exactly as on a requirement, carrying the term headword and aliases through the successor and amend shapes.
requirements.why: A shift in a term's meaning must supersede or revise-with-bump, never silently redefine; excluding TERM ids from the lifecycle machinery would leave meaning changes untracked.

requirements.statement: If spec amend targets a requirement with at least one bound @spec tag, then it shall refuse — amendment is permitted only for a Draft entry or an Active entry with zero bound tags.
requirements.why: amend rewrites in place with no version bump; amending a tagged requirement would silently mutate shipped truth out from under the @spec tags that verify it, with no supersede trail recording the change.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec move emits any version — supersede's --json spec_version, move's source and target versions, or the persisted supersededAtVersion stamp — it shall take that number from the freshly-reindexed supersede history, never an incremented authored counter.
requirements.why: A self-incremented number would let the version a lineage records diverge from the derived number pins, drift, and gate compare against — resurrecting the two-sources-of-truth split the derived model closes.

requirements.statement: When spec req <KEY> --text runs, it shall append a new Active entry — the given statement, why null when unset, empty relates/livesIn/issues unless flags fill them, no authored version counter — and bump the envelope's updated to the local date, such that reindexing yields zero diagnostics.
requirements.why: Authoring must produce exactly what the indexer ingests, or authored requirements silently vanish from coverage the moment the index rebuilds.

requirements.statement: When a lifecycle command is invoked through any surface, the spec engine shall run every guard before the first byte is written.
requirements.why: A half-applied supersede, move, deprecate, or term edit leaves one envelope flipped and the other unwritten, and no surface can tell a refused change from a partial one.

requirements.statement: When spec req <KEY> --text runs with --draft, the spec CLI shall append the new entry with status draft, writing every other field exactly as the Active path writes it.
requirements.why: An unreviewed candidate needs a status of its own, so a harvest can record a promise nobody has accepted yet without it reading as standing truth.

requirements.statement: When spec accept runs on a Draft requirement, the spec CLI shall set the entry's status to active and leave every other field byte-identical.
requirements.why: Accepting a draft is the redline decision; it must change the status and nothing the reviewer read.

requirements.statement: If spec accept targets a requirement that is not Draft, then the spec CLI shall refuse with exit 2 and write nothing.
requirements.why: Only a draft awaits acceptance; an Active, superseded or deprecated entry changes through amend, supersede or deprecate.

requirements.statement: When an authoring command receives --lives, the spec CLI shall build livesIn from every --lives occurrence, splitting each value on commas, trimming, and dropping empty entries.
requirements.why: A requirement is often implemented in several places; a flag that keeps only one path forces the rest out of the record.
requirements.deprecatedReason: Code tags are the only record of where a requirement is implemented and verified, so the authored livesIn and verifiedIn fields and everything built on them are retired.

requirements.statement: When spec amend or spec supersede or spec move receives --lives, the spec CLI shall replace the target's livesIn with that list, and an empty --lives value shall clear it.
requirements.why: One replace-or-clear idiom, the same as --aliases, so an author always knows what the stored list will be.

requirements.statement: If spec amend changes the statement or why of a requirement present in its domain file at the newest v* tag merged into HEAD, then it shall refuse with exit 2.
requirements.why: A released promise is what adopters pinned and tested; rewriting it in place leaves no supersede trail, while refusing before release churns ids for wording fixes.

requirements.statement: When spec amend refuses a released requirement, it shall name the release tag, spec supersede as the path for the promise, and --lives or --relates as the path for metadata.
requirements.why: A refusal that names no exit sends adopters to a codemod outside the validated seam.

requirements.statement: When spec amend changes only livesIn or relates of a released requirement, it shall write the change in place.
requirements.why: Location and cross-references are not the promise; a file move otherwise churns ids and rewrites every tag site.

requirements.statement: If no v* tag is merged into HEAD or the platform is not a git repository, then spec amend shall treat every requirement as unreleased.
requirements.why: Nothing is pinned before the first release, so an in-place fix costs nothing and a forced supersede only churns ids.

requirements.statement: When a lifecycle command targets an id whose prefix names no domain file holding that entry, the spec CLI shall locate the entry by scanning every domain file.
requirements.why: An id minted or moved under another key is otherwise unreachable by every command, forcing adopters to remint by codemod outside the validated seam.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede targets an entry held in a domain other than its prefix, it shall mint the successor in the holding domain.
requirements.why: The successor belongs to the charter that holds the promise, not to a key that no longer exists.

requirements.statement: When a requirement is authored or amended through the CLI, the HTTP API, or the MCP server with a relates list, the spec engine shall build relates from every entry, splitting each value on commas and trimming.
requirements.why: Cross-references the engine accepts but no surface forwards can only be authored by scripts outside the validating seam.

requirements.statement: When a requirement is amended or superseded through the CLI, the HTTP API, or the MCP server with a relates list, the spec engine shall replace the target's relates with that list, an empty list clearing it.
requirements.why: One idiom for both lists keeps livesIn and relates authoring interchangeable; a diverging rule is a surprise at the write seam.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec move mints a successor, it shall copy the predecessor's relates, every livesIn entry, cites, aliases, term, and section unless a flag overrides the field.
requirements.why: A successor that silently drops cross-references and all but the first location loses facts nobody chose to remove.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec move mints a successor, it shall carry no issues except the created row from --issue.
requirements.why: Issues are the predecessor's provenance; copying them attributes history to an entry that did not exist when it happened.

requirements.statement: When new statement text is authored into a domain that declares the ears grammar, the spec CLI shall judge it with the same EARS shape and one-promise lint spec check runs, writing with a warning under warning severity and refusing the write under error severity.
requirements.why: Catching a malformed statement at write time costs one message; catching it after code binds to the id costs a supersede.

requirements.statement: When spec amend or spec supersede or spec move receives --lives, the spec CLI shall replace the target's livesIn with that list, an empty --lives value clearing it.
requirements.why: One replace-or-clear idiom, the same as --aliases, so an author always knows what the stored list will be.
requirements.deprecatedReason: Code tags are the only record of where a requirement is implemented and verified, so the authored livesIn and verifiedIn fields and everything built on them are retired.

requirements.statement: When an authoring command receives --tests, the spec CLI shall build verifiedIn from every --tests occurrence, splitting each value on commas, trimming, and dropping empty entries.
requirements.why: A requirement is often proved by several test files; a flag that keeps only one entry forces the author to pick or to edit the file by hand.
requirements.deprecatedReason: Code tags are the only record of where a requirement is implemented and verified, so the authored livesIn and verifiedIn fields and everything built on them are retired.

requirements.statement: When spec amend or spec supersede or spec move receives --tests, the spec CLI shall replace the target's verifiedIn with that list, an empty --tests value clearing it.
requirements.why: One replace-or-clear idiom, the same as --lives, so an author always knows what a repeated flag does to the list.
requirements.deprecatedReason: Code tags are the only record of where a requirement is implemented and verified, so the authored livesIn and verifiedIn fields and everything built on them are retired.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec move mints a successor, it shall copy the predecessor's relates, every livesIn entry, every verifiedIn entry, cites, aliases, term, and section unless a flag overrides the field.
requirements.why: A successor that silently drops cross-references and all but the first location loses facts nobody chose to remove.

requirements.statement: When spec amend changes only livesIn, verifiedIn, or relates of a released requirement, it shall write the change in place.
requirements.why: Location and cross-references are not the promise; a file move otherwise churns ids and rewrites every tag site.

requirements.statement: When a new statement breaks a rule graded error, spec req, amend, supersede, move, and accept shall refuse with exit 2 and print each finding.
requirements.why: A rule that only reports after the write lets every bad statement into the book, and the sweep never ends.

requirements.statement: When spec req runs with --text, the spec CLI shall append an Active entry holding the given statement and set the domain's updated date to today.
requirements.why: Authoring must produce exactly what the indexer ingests, or authored requirements silently vanish from coverage the moment the index rebuilds.

requirements.statement: When spec amend refuses a released requirement, the spec CLI shall name the release tag, spec supersede as the path for the promise, and --relates or --issue as the path for metadata.
requirements.why: A refusal that names no exit sends adopters to a codemod outside the validated seam.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec move mints a successor, the spec CLI shall copy the predecessor's relates, cites, aliases, term, and section unless a flag overrides the field.
requirements.why: A successor that silently drops cross-references or term fields loses facts nobody chose to remove.

requirements.statement: When spec amend changes only the relates or issue links of a released requirement, the spec CLI shall write the change in place.
requirements.why: Cross-references and issue links are not the promise, so changing them must not churn the id and every tag site.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede replaces a requirement, the spec engine shall rewrite every tag of the predecessor to name the successor, keeping the tag's level token.
requirements.why: A tag left on the predecessor reports as a superseded reference, and a person retagging by hand misses sites or drops the level.

requirements.statement: When spec move replaces a requirement with one in another domain, the spec engine shall rewrite every tag of the predecessor to name the successor, keeping the tag's level token.
requirements.why: A tag left on the moved requirement reports as a superseded reference, and a person retagging by hand misses sites or drops the level.

requirements.statement: When spec deprecate ends a requirement, the spec engine shall remove every tag of that requirement.
requirements.why: A tag left on a deprecated requirement reports as a deprecated reference until someone finds and deletes it by hand.

requirements.statement: When spec deprecate is run with a reason on an Active or Draft requirement, the spec CLI shall set the entry's status to deprecated and record the reason on the entry.
requirements.why: Without a command, end-of-life was a hand edit with the reason lost in a code comment that dies with the code — the entry itself is the only place the reason survives deletion.

requirements.statement: When a new statement breaks a rule graded warning, spec req, amend, supersede, move, and accept shall write the statement and print each finding on stderr.
requirements.why: A team sweeping an existing book needs to keep authoring while the old statements are fixed, without turning the rule off everywhere.

requirements.statement: When spec deprecate runs with a reason on an Active or Draft requirement, it shall mark the entry deprecated with that reason recorded on it.
requirements.why: Without a command, end-of-life was a hand edit with the reason lost in a code comment that dies with the code — the entry itself is the only place the reason survives deletion.

requirements.statement: If a spec command runs in a directory with no spec-engine/ directory, then it shall print the not-a-platform guidance and exit 2.
requirements.why: A raw throw at the platform boundary buries the fix; exit 2 keeps the usage error distinct from the exit-1 code CI reserves for check --ci gate failures.

requirements.statement: Every spec authoring command shall exit with 0 or 2 only, never 1.
requirements.why: A CI script branching on exit codes would misread an authoring usage error as a spec-gate failure if the authoring surface ever emitted exit 1.

requirements.statement: When a statement or why holds an @ followed by a relative path containing a slash, the spec engine shall treat it as a file reference resolved from the platform root.
requirements.why: Requirement text points at code; a looser pattern would flag everyday @ usage (emails, tags, pins) as broken file references and drown the real ones in noise.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec move reports a version, it shall report the derived domain version after the change.
requirements.why: A self-incremented number would let the version a lineage records diverge from the derived number pins, drift, and gate compare against — resurrecting the two-sources-of-truth split the derived model closes.

requirements.statement: If a lifecycle command refuses for any reason, then the spec engine shall leave every SPEC.json unchanged.
requirements.why: A half-applied supersede, move, deprecate, or term edit leaves one envelope flipped and the other unwritten, and no surface can tell a refused change from a partial one.

requirements.statement: When a lifecycle command targets an id held in a domain other than its prefix, it shall act on the entry where it is held.
requirements.why: An id minted or moved under another key is otherwise unreachable by every command, forcing adopters to remint by codemod outside the validated seam.

requirements.statement: When any authoring surface receives a relates list, the spec engine shall split each value on commas and trim each entry.
requirements.why: Cross-references the engine accepts but no surface forwards can only be authored by scripts outside the validating seam.

requirements.statement: When an amend, supersede, or move receives a relates list, the spec engine shall replace the target's relates with it, an empty list clearing it.
requirements.why: One idiom for both lists keeps livesIn and relates authoring interchangeable; a diverging rule is a surprise at the write seam.

requirements.statement: When spec term runs with a name and a definition, the spec engine shall append a TERM entry holding the headword, the definition, and any aliases.
requirements.why: If authoring dropped the headword or aliases, citations by name or synonym would resolve to nothing.

requirements.statement: When spec term runs without a definition, it shall print the next unused TERM id and write nothing.
requirements.why: If the id query wrote to the store, an agent probing for the next id would mint an empty term.

requirements.statement: When spec term list runs, it shall print every term with its id and status.
requirements.why: If the list omitted a term or its status, an author could mint a duplicate or cite a superseded term.

requirements.statement: When spec term revise runs with a new definition, the spec engine shall rewrite the definition in place and advance the TERM domain's version.
requirements.why: If a revision kept the version, citing requirements would never show TERM_DRIFT and would keep pointing at the old meaning.

requirements.statement: When an authored statement's words overlap an Active requirement's at or above the duplicate threshold, the spec engine shall name that requirement as a possible duplicate without refusing the write.
requirements.why: Two requirements for one behavior split coverage and drift apart; the author needs to see the overlap while the new entry is still cheap to fold.

requirements.statement: When an authoring command runs with --json, the spec CLI shall list each possible duplicate's id and score in a possible_duplicates array.
requirements.why: An agent authoring through --json reads stdout only and would never see the stderr warning.

requirements.statement: When spec supersede or spec amend targets a TERM id, the spec CLI shall carry the term headword and aliases onto the entry it writes.
requirements.why: A shift in a term's meaning must supersede or revise-with-bump, never silently redefine; excluding TERM ids from the lifecycle machinery would leave meaning changes untracked.
